alt: Three school practices read two ways. Setting: efficient teaching for functionalists, class sorting for Marxists. Hidden curriculum: conformity to shared norms versus the correspondence principle. Testing: a fair common measure versus the myth of meritocracy.
caption: The same practice means different things to each perspective.

alt: Parsons saw school as the bridge from the family, where children are judged by particularistic standards, to wider society, where universalistic standards apply and status is achieved. Below, the four roles: socialisation, social control, economic and selective.
caption: School moves children from family standards to the same standards for everyone.

alt: Two chains. Functionalist: ability and effort, measured by standardised tests and setting, lead to role allocation and social mobility. Marxist: class background predicts outcomes, belief in merit disguises this, those who fail blame themselves, and inequality looks fair.
caption: Functionalists see a meritocracy; Marxists see a myth that legitimates inequality.

alt: School mirrors the workplace: obeying teachers corresponds to obeying bosses, and working for grades rather than interest corresponds to working for wages. Bowles and Gintis call this the correspondence principle; Willis’s lads, who resisted school, challenge it.
caption: For Marxists, school rehearses the obedience that work demands.

alt: Middle-class cultural capital learned at home is rewarded at school, so success looks like merit and class advantage is disguised. Poorer families also have less digital technology, study space, tutoring and educational trips, and working-class pupils are more often placed in lower sets.
caption: Cultural and material advantages from home are turned into school success.

alt: A staffroom where senior leaders are more likely to be men and most teachers, especially in primary schools, are women, teaching pupils that men lead and women care. Six mechanisms follow: role models, subject choice, teacher expectations (Spender), peer groups, access to education and a gendered curriculum.
caption: Who leads, who teaches and what is expected all carry gender messages.

alt: Each view with one strength and three limitations. Functionalism explains investment in schooling but ignores persistent gaps and resistance. Marxism explains lasting class gaps but neglects resistance, gender, ethnicity and mobility. Feminism exposes gender inequality but faces girls now outperforming boys.
caption: The syllabus asks for strengths and limitations of every view.
